questions.q: Who did Salesforce invite to its offline City Tours?
a: The end users of the product, such as sales agents
The executives who controlled budgets
Technology journalists and analysts
Outside software developers only
questions.why: Salesforce marketed to the people who would actually use the product, not just the buyers.

questions.q: What did Salesforce find was a powerful marketing channel despite being an online business?
a: Offline events built around real customers
Printed newspaper advertisements
Cold calls to corporate executives
Television commercials during prime time
questions.why: The summary says the City Tours turned roughly 80 percent of prospects into customers.

questions.q: What does multitenancy mean in the summary's apartment-building comparison?
a: Customers share Salesforce's servers but keep their own data
Each customer gets a separate physical server
All customers share one database with no separation
The software is installed on each customer's own machines
questions.why: The model let Salesforce update every user at once and improved the experience for all.

questions.q: Which customer-friendly moves does the summary mention alongside multitenancy?
a: Public bug reports and open access to the code
Free lifetime subscriptions for early users
A money-back guarantee on every plan
Round-the-clock phone support for all customers
questions.why: Salesforce accepted short-term risk to give customers more transparency and control.

questions.q: How did Salesforce adapt its approach in Japan?
a: It marketed less aggressively and eased in with familiar Western names
It copied its American campaign almost exactly
It hired only English-speaking sales staff
It avoided working with large local companies
questions.why: The summary says Japanese customers were modest and reserved, so a slower approach worked better.
